recent_posts.title: 2/30 Days System Design Questions!
recent_posts.summary: A classic N+1 query problem is presented: a /orders endpoint fires 51 DB queries per request due to ORM lazy-loading customer data. Four solutions are compared — eager loading with a JOIN (Prisma include), DataLoader batching, Redis caching, and denormalization — each with different trade-offs for future scalability. The post frames it as a team debate exercise rather than providing a definitive answer.

recent_posts.title: Server-Driven UI: Ship Mobile Apps without App Store Review
recent_posts.summary: Server-Driven UI (SDUI) lets mobile teams ship UI changes without App Store reviews by having the backend return a JSON tree describing what to render, while the client acts as a dumb renderer. Companies like Airbnb, Netflix, Lyft, and DoorDash use this to cut experiment velocity from weeks to days. A production blueprint covers three adoption levels (minimal, partial, full), schema versioning on two axes, TanStack Query offline caching, nine production guardrails including fallbacks and capability negotiation, and clear guidance on when SDUI is the wrong choice (video players, maps, offline-critical flows, small teams).

recent_posts.title: The Complete Guide to Location Indexing: Geohash, Quadtree, Google S2, and Uber H3
recent_posts.summary: A comparison of four location indexing strategies used by major tech companies to solve the performance problem of 2D geospatial queries on large datasets. Covers Geohash (Yelp), Quadtree (Twitter), Google S2, and Uber H3, explaining the tradeoffs each approach makes. Includes a practical decision rule: cell size must be at least as large as the search radius to avoid silently missing edge-case results at scale.

recent_posts.title: Circuit Breaker Explained
recent_posts.summary: A real-world incident postmortem where a single slow payment service caused six unrelated services to go down within two minutes. The root cause was retry logic without circuit breakers — each of 12 upstream callers retried 3 times with backoff, multiplying load 4x and creating a self-inflicted DDoS. The fix involved wrapping every outbound call in a circuit breaker (opossum for Node.js, resilience4j for Java), allowing retries only inside a closed circuit with jitter, and capping retry budgets per request chain. Key lesson: circuit breakers must come before retries, never retry through an open circuit.

recent_posts.title: Push VS Poll
recent_posts.summary: A practical framework comparing push vs pull communication patterns in distributed systems across five dimensions: consumer control (backpressure), latency, failure modes, fan-out scaling, and infrastructure cost. Push gives producers control and low latency but risks overwhelming consumers and multiplying retry complexity at scale. Pull gives consumers control with natural backpressure but can fail silently if consumers stop reading. Real-world examples include webhooks vs Kafka for event buses, and StatsD vs Prometheus for observability. Decision guidelines are provided for each pattern, with a note that most production systems use a hybrid approach (CDC pushing to Kafka, consumers pulling from Kafka).

recent_posts.title: SQS VS SNS VS EventBridge
recent_posts.summary: A practical comparison of three AWS messaging services — SQS, SNS, and EventBridge — focused on five key properties: delivery model, ordering, filtering, replay, and schema awareness. SQS suits point-to-point buffering with optional FIFO ordering. SNS enables low-latency fan-out pub/sub, commonly paired with SQS queues for per-consumer buffering. EventBridge handles complex cross-service routing, schema validation, and archive-and-replay at scale but with higher latency and cost. A decision cheat sheet maps common use cases to the right service.

recent_posts.title: AWS Lambda Aliases & Versions
recent_posts.summary: AWS Lambda Versions and Aliases are often overlooked features that enable safe, zero-downtime deployments. Versions create immutable snapshots of function code and config, while Aliases act as named pointers to those versions. The key capability is weighted traffic routing, enabling true canary deployments — e.g., sending 90% of traffic to one version and 10% to a new one — without infrastructure changes. A recommended pattern separates $LATEST for dev/testing, numbered immutable versions for releases, and named aliases like 'prod' and 'canary' for traffic control. Pointing production directly at $LATEST is flagged as a risky anti-pattern.

recent_posts.title: The Outbox Pattern
recent_posts.summary: The dual write problem occurs when saving to a database and publishing to a message broker are two separate non-atomic operations — a crash between them leaves your systems permanently out of sync. The Outbox Pattern solves this by inserting the event into an outbox table within the same database transaction as the business write, then using a separate publisher process (a poller or Debezium tailing the WAL) to relay events to Kafka. This guarantees atomicity at the write side. The key tradeoff is at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so consumers must be idempotent using the outbox row ID as a dedup key. Distributed transactions (2PC) are not a viable alternative for event-driven systems.

recent_posts.title: AWS Lambda Powertools
recent_posts.summary: Duplicates are a guaranteed property of distributed systems on AWS — SQS retries, API Gateway client retries, EventBridge retries, and Lambda async retries all produce them. AWS Lambda Powertools' idempotency utility solves this using DynamoDB as a persistence layer with a simple Python decorator. The flow extracts an idempotency key via JMESPath, uses conditional DynamoDB writes to track IN_PROGRESS and COMPLETED states, and returns cached results for duplicate events. Common mistakes include using Lambda's requestId or SQS receiptHandle as keys. The right approach is combining business identity fields like merchant_id and client_request_id, with TTL set to match the retry window (24 hours to 7 days for payments).

recent_posts.title: DynamoDB Indexes GSI VS LSI
recent_posts.summary: A practical breakdown of DynamoDB's two index types — Local Secondary Index (LSI) and Global Secondary Index (GSI) — covering their key differences, hidden gotchas, and when to use each. LSIs must be created at table creation time, support strongly consistent reads, but have a hard 10 GB per-partition limit that can silently cause write failures. GSIs can be added anytime and have no size limit, but only support eventual consistency and can throttle the base table if their write capacity is under-provisioned. AWS itself recommends GSIs in most cases. A decision framework is provided to guide the choice based on access patterns, consistency requirements, and data growth expectations.

top_posts.title: Lambda Cold Start
top_posts.summary: Since August 2025, AWS bills the Lambda INIT phase, turning cold starts from a latency nuisance into a real cost problem. Benchmarks show up to a 22x cost increase per million invocations for functions with heavy initialization. Practical mitigations include trimming deployment packages, lazy-loading non-critical SDKs, increasing memory allocation for faster CPU, and avoiding unnecessary VPC attachment. SnapStart is highlighted as an underused feature that caches initialized environments, reducing Java cold starts from 40 seconds to ~594ms, now supporting Java 11+, Python 3.12+, and .NET 8+. Provisioned Concurrency remains the right choice only for strict SLA user-facing APIs, while SnapStart plus optimization covers most other cases at far lower cost.
